newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico peso fights back but still ends off.
newsitem.headline: Mexico peso fights back but still ends off.

text.p: The Mexican peso recovered some ground lost to return to below its support at 7.80 per dollar by the close on Wednesday, but was still reeling from an early speculative onslaught, traders said.
"There were dealers who had surplus dollar positions and began to sell them when they saw the peso was recovering," a trader said, explaining the fight-back from early session lows.
The benchmark 48-hour peso and the 24-hour contract closed 5.6 and 5.9 centavos weaker, respectively, at 7.7800/7.7850 and 7.7750/7.7950 per dollar.

The same-day peso had earlier closed 6.5 centavos weaker at 7.7850/7.8000 per dollar.Traders said that foreign buyers stepping into the Mexican stock market also prompted local dealers to sell dollars.
The 48-hour peso earlier reached its weakest level this year, at 7.8250/7.8450 per dollar, as panic and speculation seized the market in early trade.

Traders said expectations that Tuesday night's substantial primary interest rate hikes might shore up the peso were dashed when traders realized that those holding dollars were not very willing to part with them in an uncertain situation.

The market was already nervous as the peso had weakened considerably in recent sessions and foreign investors had shunned the Mexican markets following a watering down in the government's petrochemical privatization plans.
Other traders pointed to comments made by U.S. economist and MIT professor Rudiger Dornbusch to the local press criticising the cental bank's policies.
"Banco de Mexico is bad news for the peso, not people who predict there will be difficulties," Dornbusch was quoted as saying on the front page of the Reforma newspaper, which many traders read.
In a Reuters interview, Dornbusch said he had not accused the Banco de Mexico of intervening directly in the currency markets, but of using monetary policy as a brake on peso depreciation.

"I have not said that (Banco de Mexico has intervened in the currency market directly). I said that if you allow me to control the (monetary) aggregates, I control the interest rates, which controls the peso," he said.

On Monday, Banco de Mexico had announced it would allow the secondary money market to close on Tuesday with a liquidity shortfall of 20 million pesos, as opposed to balancing liquidity flows exactly, as it had done since August 16.
Many traders saw this move as designed to push up interest rates and shore up the peso, which had already begun to totter.
Dornbusch said this move was valid as a temporary move, but should not aim to help the peso recoup lost ground.
"That is alright for a brief moment, just to stabilize expectations and to say we are not looking for big drop... But if they want to bring the peso back, that is lunacy," he said.

Traders said they did not spot any central bank intervention in the market on Wednesday, although several said they expected the Banco de Mexico to step in selling dollars if the peso nudged up to levels around 7.85 per dollar.
